THYROID EMERGENCIES 
 
 
HYPERTHYROIDISM 
* History: Fatigue, palpitations, heat intolerance, anxiety, weight loss 
despite increased appetite, pathological fractures 2nd to 
osteoporosis. May be misdiagnosed as psychological condition 
* Examination: Tremor, pre-tibial oedema, proptosis/peri-orbital oedema, 
lid lag, proximal myopathy, high output cardiac failure, 
goitre or thyroid nodules 
* Vital signs: Sinus tachycardia/new AF, hypertension, increased 
temperature 
* Causes: Graves’ disease, thyroid tumours, multinodular goitre, 
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, TSH producing pituitary tumour, 
pregnancy related (Molar pregnancy), drug induced e.g. 
amiodarone, levothyroxine overtreatment 
* Differential diagnosis: Sepsis; heat stroke; anticholinergic / 
sympathomimetic drug intoxication; malignant 
hyperthermia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome; 
serotonergic syndrome; delirium tremens / 
withdrawal; pheochromocytoma; psychiatric / 
psychological conditions (diagnosis of exclusion) 
* Biochemistry: Usually high T3/T4, low TSH, except TSH producing pituitary 
conditions. Concomitant adrenal insufficiency – 
hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia 
* Risk stratification: Burch-Wartofsky scale to assess risk of Thyroid storm 
• ACUTE MANAGEMENT: 
Identify precipitant, screen and manage complications e.g. AF, consult 
endocrine to start antithyroid Rx/further workup 
• THERAPY: 
Carbimazole (Neo-mercazole) 20-60mg dly, titrate to effect. Propranolol 
40mg bd for symptom control. Definitive Rx Radioactive Iodine therapy 
 
 
 
HYPOTHYROIDISM 
*History: Fatigue/lethargy, cold intolerance, weight gain, cognitive 
impairment/slowed mentation, depression, coarse features, 
constipation. High index of suspicion in elderly, depressed pts 
*Examination: Dry skin, coarse hair, slowed speech/movement, pallor, 
hair loss, goitre, hoarseness, non-pitting oedema 
(myxoedema) 
* Vital signs: Bradycardia, hypotension, decreased temperature 
*Causes: Autoimmune thyroiditis, previous thyroid surgery/radioactive 
iodine treatment, dietary iodine deficiency, drug induced, 
pituitary pathology 
*Differential diagnosis: Sepsis; hypothermia, cardiac arrhythmias e.g. 
3rd degree heart block, slow AF; dementia; 
sedative intoxication; psychiatric/psychological 
conditions 
*Biochemistry: Usually low T3/T4, high TSH 
*Risk stratification: Screen for features of impending myxoedema coma 
*ACUTE MANAGEMENT: 
Identify precipitant, screen and manage complications e.g. 
hypothermia. Consult endocrine to initiate thyroid hormone 
replacement 
*THERAPY: 
Levothyroxine (Eltroxin) 50-100g dly

THYROID STORM 
*Life threatening endocrine emergency, high 
mortality 
*Features of severe thyrotoxicosis AND altered 
mental status 
*Precipitants: Trauma, infection, DKA, CVA, MI, 
drug induced, radioactive iodine therapy, non- 
compliance; pregnancy related 
*A clinical diagnosis ➔ do not wait for blood results 
*Calculate the Burch-Wartofsky Score 
(available online at MDCalc) 
*Consult Endocrine EARLY to co-manage 
ACUTE ED MANAGEMENT: 
• Rapid triage to resus, monitors, IV access 
• Benzodiazepines PRN for agitation 
• Active cooling measures, paracetamol ➔ Avoid 
salicylates 
• Fluid resus 20ml/kg crystalloid boluses prn 
• B-blocker *Caution in ADHF*: 
Propranolol 60-80 mg po 4hrly, OR 
Esmolol 250-500g/kg IV load over 1 min, then 50- 
100 g/kg/min IV 
• Methimazole 20-30mg PO 6hrly, OR 
Propylthiouracil 600-1000mg PO load, then 300mg 
PO 6hrly (max 1.2g/day) 
• Hydrocortisone 100mg IV stat then q8hrly OR 
Dexamethasone 2-4mg q6hrly 
• Lugol’s iodine 4-8 drops PO 6hrly – 60 minutes AFTER 
PTU/methimazole 
If Iodine allergy ➔ Li Carbonate 300mg 6 hrly 
• Consider antibiotics and sepsis workup 
• Plasmapheresis as last resort if no response to 
treatment 
 
 
Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale 
 
 
MYXOEDEMA COMA 
*Extreme hypothyroidism with cardiovascular 
collapse, high mortality 
*Commonly precipitated by sepsis 
*Profound stupor/coma, hypothermia, 
bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, 
respiratory failure, non-pitting oedema, 
hyponatraemia, 
*Suspect in elderly/ comatose/ hypothermic/ 
bradycardic pts 
*Consult Endocrine EARLY 
ACUTE ED MANAGEMENT: 
*Rapid triage to resus, monitors, IV access 
*ABC resuscitation 
*May require intubation, fluid resuscitation, pacing, 
gentle active warming 
*Caution when commencing inotropes – may 
paradoxically decompensate 
*Correct hypoglycaemia and electrolyte abnormalities 
– hyponatraemia common 
*Cautious Na+ correction, <10mmol/L/day, unless 
actively fitting – see Hyponatraemia protocol 
*Solucortef 100mg q8hrly if adrenal/pituitary 
insufficiency suspected 
*Thyroid hormone replacement: 
Levothyroxine (Eltroxin) 300 – 500g (6g/kg IBW) 
IV load, then 50g dly (oral via NGT if no IV available) 
*Investigate and manage precipitant
